transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump campaigned for Republican candidates in Ohio yesterday, with just weeks to go before the midterm elections.
Jerry Kenney of member station WYSO reports Trump's visit was the latest in a series of campaign stops across the country.
He played all his greatest hits to an enthusiastic capacity crowd, citing what he called his administration's accomplishments,
including a "strong tariff policy" and stopping illegal immigration. He also brought up data centers, a controversial issue for some Ohio cities.
We're also taking historic action to ensure that big tech data centers benefit local communities.
We want them, look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio.
Trump was stumping in Vandalia for incumbent Republican Senate candidate John Husted. Husted is in a tight race against former Ohio Democratic senators Sherrod Brown.
For NPR News, I'm Jerry Kenney in Yellow Springs.
The U.S. Coast Guard is continuing its search for a Canadian medical transport plane after crews located a debris field off the coast of Nantucket.
NPR's Frank Langford reports the plane disappeared yesterday morning while flying from Bermuda to Boston.
The Gulfstream G-100 is believed to have been carrying six people on board when it lost contact with air traffic control, according to the Coast Guard.
Flight data show the jet dropped at least 9,000 feet over two minutes, then leveled off for several more minutes before disappearing.
The pilot declared an emergency, according to Nantucket Memorial Airport.
During an exchange, air traffic control asked the pilot of the air ambulance, quote, "You're coming in blind?"
A fire rescue dispatcher warned emergency crews.
The plane was suffering from electrical issues and had lost radio and radar, according to audio on broadcastify, and that was also reviewed by the Boston Globe.
The Coast Guard has deployed two search and rescue planes, as well as a helicopter and a motor lifeboat.
Frank Langford, NPR News.
The U.S. Supreme Court opens a new term this week, and PR's Nina Totenberg reports the justices have a full docket.
Even as the justices will hear major cases on climate change, immigration, guns and religion, there are many more hot-button issues waiting in the wings.
Among them, whether the court will reverse nearly a half-century-old precedent that bars the posting of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
More immediately, though, the justices are likely to be drawn into the election.
The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and Democrats have lawyers across the country ready to fight what they perceive as illegal measures.
In the end, though, some of these clashes are bound to make it to the Supreme Court.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News.
The tree that was chosen for this year's Capitol Christmas display in Washington, D.C., is being replaced because of needle-cast disease.
Lauren Patterson reports officials in Idaho say the change won't delay the festivities.
The original 80-foot-tall grand fir was monitored over the summer, and yellowed needles means it didn't make the cut.
The possibility that the number-one choice might have been a problem is why U.S. Forest Service officials always have a backup.
Zachary Peterson is a staff officer for the Nezper's Clearwater National Forests.
"We want our plans to go with our backup tree, which is Angelman Spruce, 7 6 feet tall, very similar in size, very similar in shape on the Waksau Power Ranger cluster."
The spruce will be harvested in late October.
The tree will be packaged up and sent on a whistle-stop tour throughout Idaho before its journey to Washington, D.C.
For NPR News, I'm Lauren Patterson in Kami'i, Idaho.
President Trump has posted Senator Tom Cotton's personal cell phone number online, urging people to call the Arkansas Republican over his opposition to permanent daylight saving time.
Trump wants the Senate to pass the Sunshine Protection Act, which cleared the House in July.
Cotton is among the Republican senators who oppose it.
Trump argued yesterday that the change would give Americans more daylight when they're most active.
Cotton says it would make winter a "dark and dismal time."
Legislation to make the change has gone back and forth between the two chambers for years.
This is NPR News.
